idiom_name: message-carried itinerary + slip-aware dispatcher + step registry
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define the slip as an ordered list of step identifiers (or destinations) living in the message envelope next to a progress marker, and define a step as a function taking the envelope (plus context) and returning success or failure with the possibly enriched envelope. One planner computes the list for the message; a small dispatcher, invoked at each step boundary, resolves the current entry through a registry, calls it and advances the marker before routing the message to the next entry. The dispatcher owns the routing mechanics so that steps never name their successors, and the registry keeps physical endpoint addresses out of the slip. Because delivery between steps is not transactional, every step has to be idempotent and record compensation data for effects that cannot simply be retried.
code_sketch:
envelope = { body, slip: ["validate", "reserve", "charge"], cursor: 0 }

loop:
    if envelope.cursor == len(envelope.slip): finish(envelope); break
    step = registry[envelope.slip[envelope.cursor]]      # whitelist lookup
    outcome = step.execute(envelope)                     # idempotent + undo data
    if outcome.failed: compensate_or_dead_letter(envelope, outcome); break
    envelope.cursor += 1
    channel.send(destination_of(envelope.slip, envelope.cursor), envelope)
pitfalls: Letting each step decide its own successor puts the route back into code; the slip (or its planner) must own the order.
Without validation of the itinerary, anyone able to set the header chooses which components process the message.
Retrying a step that is not idempotent and records no undo data duplicates business effects, because the pattern offers no transaction.

Wrong move: use a precomputed slip when the next hop depends on intermediate results or must branch/parallelise -> the fixed linear itinerary cannot adapt safely -> instead use a Dynamic Router or Process Manager.
